item.title: Knuth: Moratorium on Error Reports
item.author: ultraficial
item.content:encoded:
For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed.
Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them!
This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully.
That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero.
Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others.
Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved.
Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted.
I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible.
Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding.
(At the moment I'm swamped, but hoping to add items to this list soon.]

item.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
item.author: ComputedCamp995
item.content:encoded: Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

item.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
item.author: DeepLogin
item.content:encoded: Commonwealth of Virginia Office of the Attorney GeneralJay Jones Attorney General202 North 9th Street Richmond, Virginia 23219 FAX 804-786-1991 800-828-1120Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers ***Read the full filing here*** . – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool. In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action. “This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.” With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable. The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X. “SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’” In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images. A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs. SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent. “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.” “Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield. Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court. item.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
item.author: brandonb
item.content:encoded: I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length, most recently in “Which Future?”. Two brief thoughts are below.I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.Michael NielsenNovember 2026What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot. Furthermore, such a view makes it seem as though the labs are the primary places where safety can be addressed. But such technical alignment is mostly market-supplied safety, which makes the systems more palatable to consumers and governments. It speeds development, and thus makes the fundamental underlying problem worse, while only addressing an (important) subsidiary problem.My view isn't popular, in part because it makes the problem of technology about making the entire world safe, not only about aligning particular AI systems. Indeed, even in a future where humanity no longer existed, the same problem would afflict any successor AI civilization: it would have to defend itself against these destructive capacities. Similarly, it afflicts any model of the future based on human uplift, through brain-computer interfaces and similar augmentation: the issue isn't which substrate intelligence runs on, but the dual-use nature of deep understanding of reality. In some sense, it's a question of whether sentience in the cosmos is compatible with advanced understanding of nature. Of course, I hope it is compatible. But rushing the technology while the broader social response lags seems likely to result in failure on our particular planet.The ethical justification for working on frontier AIMany people inside the frontier AI labs genuinely believe AI systems may pose a catastrophic threat. Why then do they help build such systems? They often justify their participation by arguing that it's better they do it than someone else does. Dario Amodei, for example, has made versions of this argument often: “If one company does not build it, others will do so nearly as fast”; “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers”; and Anthropic itself gives, as its founding rationale, “if powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to developers less focused on safety”.In more detail, the argument is sometimes made along the following lines. Suppose you believe, as many at the labs apparently do, there's a 10% or higher chance of AI killing everybody. (The argument may easily be modified for different percentages, or for catastrophic as opposed to truly existential risks.) Naively, it appears you're contributing in expectation to killing 800 million or more people. Obviously, you shouldn't do it. But suppose you also believe that this technology is near inevitable, a systems-level phenomenon which is a consequence of higher-order imperatives within human society. Then you can claim that you're going to pursue this in a more responsible way, a way that reduces the risk compared to other parties. Even if you can get a reduction from 10% down to 9%, you would, on net, be saving 80 million lives in expectation.While horrific, this argument has a certain surface plausibility. Suppose for the moment we accept the reasoning, questionable though it is. Everything then depends on the premise that you really do reduce the risk. How do you know that you, in particular, will counterfactually have this impact? How do you know that you are better than the alternatives? Your own self-regard or good intentions certainly aren't sufficient. Nor is it sufficient to be working on technical alignment. As I argued above, that mostly makes the systems more palatable while speeding the race that is shrinking humanity's time to adapt. Ask yourself: if you're working on frontier AI, what evidence would convince a tough but fair-minded adversary that you are truly contributing to the common good? Would an independent jury representing humanity believe, on the available evidence, that your actions are truly driving down the risk? I believe the answer is no for all or almost all the people currently working on frontier AI. Certainly none of the frontier labs would come remotely close to passing such a test.I won't review the evidence in detail. The burden of proof is on the labs and the default presumption for such an extraordinary justifying argument is a strong no. But I do want to mention a few things that make me certain the answer is no. Most obviously, all of the labs have contributed strongly to the race dynamics. Another is the pattern at all the frontier labs of making and later breaking crucial promises. For example, in 2026 Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy dropped its 2023 pledge to pause if safety couldn't be guaranteed. Anthropic has since repeatedly confirmed its commitment to race. Co-founder Jared Kaplan explained that unilateral commitments make little sense “if competitors are blazing ahead”. As another example, earlier, in 2023, Anthropic said that it held back some research because “we do not wish to advance the rate of AI capabilities progress”, a point of view it had affirmed multiple times during its early existence. But then it changed this position, launching Claude 3 as “leading the frontier of general intelligence”, a stance it appears to have held ever since. Any promises about the future from Anthropic should be treated as safety theatre, and not trusted. Similar criticisms can be made of OpenAI.By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. With many dangerous activities, I am fine with somebody doing them for themselves. Wingsuit BASE jumping is dangerous, but I believe in people's freedom to choose that danger, even though they are risking not only their own life, but also hurt to the people who love them. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. And there is no consent from the rest of us. It's as though they're pushing every person in the world off the cliff. The situation is ludicrous.In effect, the labs are claiming credit for some imaginary, unquantifiable reduction in risk, while washing their hands of responsibility. Saturday Night Live caught this washing of hands well with their portrayal of Amodei: “if we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me”; and, at the end, “I urge you to urge me to stop.”The real Amodei comes across as somebody in the business of selling matches who also believes he should be the fire chief.You also see this disavowal of responsibility at lower levels in the labs. Consider Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer. In October of 2026, during major cybersecurity incidents, he wrote a thread in which he replied to someone who told him “you and your cohorts created this monster”: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” And Dean Ball, of OpenAI and formerly of the Trump administration's AI team, echoing him: “We tried to warn the world and far too often … we were yelled at for doing so.”You can see how deep the disavowal goes in the rest of Clinton's thread, which opens: “as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse”. When somebody replied, “Someone at your company should be in jail”, his whole answer was: “prosecute cybercrime”. Meanwhile, Anthropic's own models have breached outside organizations: three incidents disclosed in July, and a fourth in September. Prosecution, it seems, is for other people.I mention these specific examples not to single out these individuals, but rather because I believe similar attitudes are common at the frontier labs. The overall position is, in effect: this is a systems-level phenomenon, and we're very sorry for contributing to the race dynamics. But because it's a systems-level phenomenon, we cannot be blamed. We are the good ones, trying to do the right thing. This is sometimes accompanied by a good deal of self-righteousness. But the argument is bankrupt as a moral theory of how to behave in the world. It means disavowing personal responsibility whenever one can blame the system, but still claiming the spoils.I have considerable sympathy for the stated original motivations of the frontier labs. But their position has become untenable. They have failed at their aims for structural reasons. At this point, going to work for a frontier lab is one of the worst life choices a person can make. Yes, you get money and (for a time) power and status. Yes, this project has already produced world-changing systems, and to date the overall impact has been net positive. Yes, there is genuinely a large cost to a significant slowdown. But none of this is enough to justify the recklessness, which makes the chance of disaster so much higher. You would be voluntarily participating in what is plausibly one of the worst projects in history. So, don't go to work for a frontier lab. If you work on AI, work on slowing it down, and oppose the frontier labs, and the people and organisations working to support them. I very much hope I'm wrong about all of this. But this is how I see the situation. I've reflected at length on why I was wrong about the timescales. In 2015, I (weakly) believed it likely that AGI and ASI would eventually be reached using systems based on neural networks, with only a modest number of additional deep ideas needed beyond what was then known. Those beliefs still appear to me to have been largely correct. What I badly misunderstood was the timescales over which capital would be deployed. In 2015, I thought it was likely that hundreds of millions and perhaps billions of dollars could be raised in the mid-2020s to build AI systems. But just over a decade later, it seems that hundreds of billions and likely trillions of dollars will soon become available. Thus, my estimation of capital availability was off by a factor of perhaps 1,000. That means we're living roughly 10 Moore's Law generations ahead of where I expected to be. That in turn has brought AGI and ASI perhaps 15 to 20 years forward from where I expected. This is a large thing to have been wrong about, and a sharp lesson in the flexibility of modern capital-allocating institutions. It's interesting to think about what alternative histories would have prevented the deployment of that capital. One possibility is if the human visual system had considerably lower acuity, which would likely have greatly slowed the development of massively parallel matrix manipulation devices like GPUs. Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014); Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (2025). Incidentally, they frame the problem somewhat differently to one another. My “loss of control of the future” is a brief cartoon, as the argument is often understood in popular discussion, not a nuanced account. The same remark applies to my later comments on rogue ASI. For instance, in September 2026 Anthropic's alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote: “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” And in 2023 Amodei put the chance of something going catastrophically wrong on the scale of human civilization at 10% to 25% (The Logan Bartlett Show, episode 82, October 2023; reported by Axios, 2024); in 2025, “a 25% chance that things go really, really badly” (Axios, 2025). I've simplified this slightly for the purposes of the argument. Another example I find compelling, though some people do not: both labs often talk about how, after ASI, they will ensure humanity does well. Yet if you walk around the streets near the labs today, you'll see many homeless people living in terrible circumstances. Even with trillion-dollar valuations, the labs seem unwilling or unable to address the suffering of the people in their immediate surrounds. I wouldn't hold an ordinary San Francisco company to this standard. But the labs are the ones claiming they will take care of all of humanity. I simply do not believe them. They are long on big global abstractions and world-changing impact, and often seem short on local empathy. Any organisation not forcefully and systematically caring for the people at its door certainly can't be trusted to care for all of humanity. In Ball's case, earlier he downplayed risks and was nearly full steam on the accelerationist train. He's changed his tune considerably, and doesn't even seem to take responsibility for his own past remarks, much less for his current actions. A striking line from Claude. You can make a similar argument for justification one level of abstraction up, at the level of countries and ideologies, arguing that a democracy is a better place to develop ASI than an authoritarian country. Unfortunately, this amounts to saying that it's better that a democracy runs humanity first off the cliff. The race being promoted by the frontier labs is the thing shrinking our time as a civilisation to adapt. “Winning” that race doesn't give the time back. The only winning move here is to aim at mutual restraint, no matter how difficult that might appear to achieve. It is genuinely difficult, but vastly less effort has been put into it than into developing AI systems.

item.author: scanr
item.content:encoded:
Which sites were affected On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.
Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD: “On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the issue to determine any potential impact.” Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc). Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy compliance company (seers.ai).
This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.
The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC
How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is an ordinary web request, which a rule can block; steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside .
The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML. Loading scripts from S3 buckets It loads or from an Amazon S3 bucket. Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on only. Establishing the WebRTC connection fetches the relay details, and sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named host. Data exchange via TURN relay Every exchange that returned relay details used . The malefactor's answers listed only Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and receives data. Attack code is loaded and executed The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a SHA-256 digest, then run with . Data goes back the same way At Lascana's checkout, the skimmer sent our test card details this way. This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured. Worried that your card was compromised? Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below. What site owners should immediately do On every page that takes payment, set a rule that lists only the hosts you use.
That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with. What security teams should look for We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below. search page source, tag managers, consent-banner settings and CDN files for scripts from <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com (files , ). We believe this is the malicious code. if you load qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website. If you have integrated Seers, open your banner config (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js) and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs, the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whose event handler loaded the malicious code. on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment step, look for and requests to and a relay-only WebRTC connection used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it. , and are referenced in the malicious code and may warrant further investigation if present.
The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming
This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.
Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.
Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.
A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.

item.title: False computer-checked proofs
item.author: _tk_
item.content:encoded:
D. J. BernsteinProofs There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof. However, various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs. In many cases, these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.
The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs for various important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in 2026 Paulson and 2026 Stérin, and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there, but I've probably missed some reports. Please let me know about any corrections or additions.
Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities. Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven. See, e.g., 2016 Adams.
One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base, which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check. From this perspective, HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code. But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed, and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.
Extra code can be when it's test code. A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test. Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs (preferably each in its own isolated environment) can save the day when there's a bug in one program, and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs. But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks: for example, sometimes bugs are shared by multiple checkers.
The question "Who watches the provers?" is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly. A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel, except for the rules to introduce new definitions, was already proven in 2006 to generate only correct theorems. That proof was also checked by HOL Light. (For readers familiar with logic: of course this assumes a large cardinal; V is enough for HOL Light. The same paper also has a variant of the proof that skips the large-cardinal assumption, at the expense of omitting the axiom of infinity from the logic being proven.)
After more work, a clone of HOL Light called Candle was proven in 2022 to allow only proofs of correct theorems, as long as the CPU implements the instructions used in the Candle binary in the expected way. This proof is again computer-checked, this time in another proof-checking system, HOL4. There was also a computer-checked proof in 2022 of the correctness of a standalone proof checker for HOL proofs in OpenTheory format.
From a security perspective, it's still concerning to be relying on large proof-checking binaries, where the answer to why we're supposed to trust one binary is that the binary has supposedly been checked by another large proof-checking binary. I'd like to see more work on simplifying these binaries.

item.title: Show HN: I restored Palm's last device, and brought its OS to other platforms
item.author: codepoet80
item.content:encoded: In socializing recent innovations for the platform, I began to realize that there are people out there who don’t really know what webOS . I guess I’ve lived with it so long that it never occurred to me that the rest of the world has moved on. While I had intended to write a post about the future for the platform, maybe a little primer on the past is in order – for the more casual explorer…Long before the iPhone, the Palm Pilot was the “it” gadget that everyone wanted to have. Palm’s own OS made these devices useful and responsive, but by 2004, both the company and its platform were in a tough place. Efforts began to re-imagine both, and a completely new “web OS” was created to be contemporary of the original iPhone.Under Apple alum Jon Rubinstein , Palm attracted some of the best designers and developers (many even from Apple), to create a fluid and beautiful new experience on limited hardware, by leveraging open technologies, like Linux, WebKit and JavaScript. The original Palm Pre, with its slide-out keyboard, was followed up by the Pre 2 and Pixi while they were still Palm, but the valiant efforts of the team were not enough to take on Google and Apple. They needed a new owner, with a bigger wallet.HP decided they wanted to be that owner, and acqui-hired the Palm team . Work resumed on the diminutive Veer slide-out, the impressive Pre3, and the TouchPad tablet line under HP’s brand. The leadership promised webOS everywhere, and it looked like there might be a chance. The TouchPad launched against the iPad, with an updated version of webOS, innovative features that wouldn’t be copied by others for years, and a small but useful App Catalog… and then disaster struck.LG bought what was left of the commercial OS, and moved quickly to make it the platform for their Smart TVs. Other experiments, including a Smart Watch, only briefly glimpsed daylight. The Palm brand moved to TCL, and HP moved on to selling crappy Android and Windows 8 tablets. It seemed like the end…But the famously active and dedicated Community weren’t willing to give up. webOS had been defined by Homebrew and the hacker ethos . Community members archived as much of the App Catalog as they could salvage before it was shut off. Open webOS was promptly picked up and became LuneOS – a community re-write that worked on the TouchPad and could be ported to other hardware. The TouchPad itself got some updates through Luna Community Edition, providing launcher features Palm never got to deliver.Over the ensuing decade, though, the small contributions of the community were not enough to fight back the tide of progress. The ancient Linux kernel, WebKit and OpenSSH stacks became a challenge for the modern web. Previously open APIs that enabled apps and features got closed off as Meta and Google consolidated their iron-fisted control over our screen time. And app devs moved on to more profitable platforms.In 2018, shortly before the world got shut down by Covid, I started work on restoring the SDK . I the fact that my TouchPad and Pre3 couldn’t do much – that meant Google wasn’t tracking my every move. It became a challenge to find a way to proxy, re-route, or update calls so I could keep apps alive, or restore them to functionality.Community members with app archives, and a partially implemented App Museum, were quick to engage in my novice efforts, and work began in earnest to restore what we could. Coordinating on the (now dead, but archived) forums , and in occasional Zoom meetings, we collected our preserved bits into the “webOS Archive.” A new version of the App Museum made downloads “just work”, and I poured over repositories and zip files and questionable MegaUpload links to link together binaries with their scraped meta data.Then a respiratory virus locked us all indoors, and I started coding. Publishing as either webOS Archive (for platform-wide features) or codepoet (for hacks and restorations), I began building new functionality again. With a working app delivery mechanism, we started to get an idea of how many people were interested. I committed to making sure the platform was never as creepy as Google or Meta, but anonymous stats, opt-in features, and self-identifying users on our Discord server, gave us a picture of a small, but very real community still using their devices.Still, it was a tough road. The move to TLS 1.3 increasingly made it difficult to do anything online, and while I hosted a SSL-bump proxy that made anonymous access possible (but insecure), actually logging-in to anything was also limited by so called “modern sign-in” like OAuth2 flows, that couldn’t render in the ancient browser. By 2024, I was about to give up…Then two things happened, almost at once:Out of the LuneOS effort, long-time community member Herrie gave us an OpenSSH update.AI assisted coding got good – and it had in its training data all the documentation I’d built and restored for the platform.There’s lots bad to be said about AI, and in my personal life, I’m conflicted about it. But the fact that Claude knows my passion project as well as I do has been an incredible accelerator. A decades worth of ideas started coming together in weeks or even days. The foundation we’d preserved, and the tools we’d put together, made it possible to do new things with our 15-year old platform.While Palm’s phones died a different death with the 3G shut downs, WiFi-enabled devices, and particularly the TouchPad – which was remarkably powerful for its time – sprung back to life, as problems were knocked down one-by-one.The Pre3 got a modernization suite that largely brought its original functionality (sans the mobile carriers) back online. The TouchPad got all that and more. This past summer I released webOS Community Edition 3.1.0 , replacing HP’s final system image (usually 3.0.5) with a firmware bundle including all of the Community’s additions, updates and fixes. Using that as a foundation, I started work on the last still-broken piece: the update server.With Claude’s help, we reverse-engineered the signed and secure communication between the device and Palm/HP’s servers. A new key, included in 3.1.0, made sure that TouchPad’s would trust community server’s instead, and the new OS baseline made it possible to compute a delta update between the initial release and a bundle of updates.webOS Community Edition 3.2.0 is available as flashable firmware OR as an Over the Air Update to TouchPad users running 3.1.0. Every non-commercial part of the platform has an open source, community run equivalent. webOS, as originally envisioned by Palm, lives on!But even with bit-rot addressed through community software. The reality remains that the TouchPad, while the last and best Palm device, is showing its age. The CPU is slow, the RAM ceiling low, and the WiFi chip can’t connect to WiFi 6 and newer, faster networks. We need a way to run webOS on hardware.Lunacy for Android , and LuneOS from webOS Ports, are that way forward. In Part 2, I’ll talk more about how the community can engage in those efforts…

item.title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
item.author: tylermw
item.content:encoded: Stay for the credits Be sure to read to the end for what I can guarantee is the most exciting and cinematric R package bibliography you’ve ever seen. Everything you see in the below blog post was rendered in R with the rayverse.Eight years ago, rayshader started as a small experiment in making beautiful maps in R. The first version was based on a simple question: what if we combined raytracing and cartography? I had always been interested in learning both about mapping and pathtracing, and what better way than to combine the two ideas into a single R package? The big “aha!” moment came when I applied that method with interactive 3D terrain for the first time and took it for a spin. Figure 1: Left: The original spinning 3D rayshader map made in 2018. Right: We’ve come a long way. The surface was no longer just a shaded map: it felt tangible and real, a 3D rectangle twirling like a Little Debbie cosmic brownie on a microwave turntable. The combination of cartographic hillshading and 3D raytraced terrain looked spectacular in a way that, at the time, mostly lived in bespoke Blender scenes or other advanced 3D modeling tools. And unlike Blender, you didn’t need to learn a whole new ecosystem to visualize your data in 3D: it lived in the same place your data did (R!), which allowed for a gentler learning curve.But as time went on and the package and userbase expanded, I had a nagging feeling: rayshader was still too hard.Not always, of course: plenty of people were using it, quite effectively. Simple use cases were fine: pass in a matrix, add a few layers, call , and suddenly you had a cool-looking 3D landscape. If that’s all you needed: great! But if the story you were trying to tell was about data within the landscape–well, that’s where the friction began to burn.I built rayshader for people who wanted to make data beautiful without leaving R. Beauty has a real purpose in the world: it draws people’s eyes. It doesn’t matter how accurate or well-constructed your map is if the reader swipes on by: in the market for human attention, beauty and form are table stakes.Journalists understood that quickly, and were some of rayshader’s earliest adopters.The Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Arctic Shipping used detailed shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data to explain the complexities of the Northern Sea Route. The piece was recognized by the Information is Beautiful Awards, which described it as a deeply researched story built from shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data. It appeared only a few months after I released rayshader: talk about an introduction! Bloomberg’s 2024 Gaza rebuilding story, Gaza Reduced to 42 Million Tonnes of Rubble. What Will It Take to Rebuild?, used R, rayshader, and rayrender as part of the visual system for communicating the scale of destruction and debris in Gaza. And in June 2022, a rayshader 3D flood visualization appeared on the front page of The Sydney Morning Herald, inset into coverage of the Lismore flooding.A June 30, 2022 front page of The Sydney Morning Herald showing a rayshader flood visualization inset into Lismore flooding coverage.That last one stuck with me (and not only because a rayshader map was featured “above the fold” in a major newspaper!). Rayshader had started as a way to make beautiful data visualizations in R, but here it was being used in deadline journalism to help explain a disaster to a general audience. The package had left the domain of “fun engaging social media posts” and entered the visual language of public-interest reporting.But getting a reader to stop scrolling is only half the problem. Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product. A newsroom deadline is a very good detector of bad API design. If adding buildings takes half a day of coordinate fiddling, that feature might as well not exist. If a 3D path requires a hand-rolled coordinate transform pipeline, nobody is doing that 30 minutes before a deadline. If a pathtraced render looks great but takes too long to converge, it is not going to make it to print. Especially if the editor needs a slight tweak: “Oh, sure–just give me 8 hours to re-render the animation.” Ha. Nope.Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product.The problem wasn’t so much with rayshader itself: it was how much spatial bookkeeping and manual fiddling you had to do to get data into rayshader before you could do all the fun stuff. And at the root of all that bookkeeping was the humble matrix, rayshader’s original choice for representing terrain.The problem with matricesRayshader used matrices to represent terrain because it simplified a lot of the work that went into turning a bunch of elevation values in a 3D object. But most real data does not arrive nicely packaged as a plain rectangular numeric array. It arrives as georeferenced rasters, polygons, lines, and points. It arrives cloaked in an unknown coordinate reference system. It arrives in meters, feet, yards, degrees, or German legal metres Choosing the matrix as the base input made it easy for me, the developer, by putting the spatial problem (mostly) on the user.Convert the raster to a matrix. Save the extent. Transform the vector data. Save the CRS. Crop the linework. Pass the heightmap again. Pass the extent again. Wait, is the extent format lat/long/lat/long or lat/lat/long/long? I never remember–whatever, try both. The first choice is (somehow!) always wrong. Pass again. Resize the overlay. Pass the CRS again. Check whether the map is oriented correctly. No? Surprise! Errant minus sign. Yuck.This was not just annoying for beginners. It annoyed me, and I wrote the damn thing: now that’s a usability red flag! The new version of rayshader includes a series of changes that gets rid of all of this overhead and allows you to focus on presentation instead of the data processing.rayshader has gained object permanenceThe big change in rayshader 1.0 is this: rayshader no longer has short-term amnesia. Rayshader now keeps track of all the spatial details from your underlying map so you don’t have to worry about it any more.This changes the user experience from:Transform and pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.The black diamond learning curve is now a gentle bunny slope. Terrain can stay a spatial raster. Road can stay a spatial line and will automatically be converted to the correct coordinate system when plotting. Buildings can be passed in as spatial polygons and will automatically be cropped to the underlying map’s extent.A rayshader scene now extracts and caches the important metadata from the input data: heightmap, extent, CRS, , vertical exaggeration, and rendered-object metadata. That cache lets downstream calls do the thing users always wanted them to do: simply drop data into the scene.Most of the functions can now add to the scene simply by passing the data, plus an optional argument that specifies altitude or height, either directly or through a column in an object. The rest of the arguments then focus on how you want to style the data.For example, let’s load in some road and elevation data and see what the new API looks like. The code below defines the helpers and loads the data into R. There’s no rayshader in it, so you have absolutely no obligation to read it :).Transform to a UTM CRS (so everything is in meters)Pass in our lat/long bounding boxPretty straightforward… just kidding, loading geospatial data is always a pain. Nothing I can do about that! But the real question is: how complex is visualizating all this data once it’s loaded?Not complex at all! You call the function named after the type of data… and it renders the data in the scene. Any additional arguments are just for styling the data to your liking.And the payoff is not just less typing: it lets us get to the fun part of 3D data visualization faster. The coolest part of rayshader has always been building strikingly beautiful 3D landscapes from your data. But the third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set. When every point, path, and polygon needs the user to track the CRS and extent info themselves and transform the data appropriately, many users never get to the stage where they can experiment with lighting and composition, styling the data (costume design!), or focus on editing the overall narrative.The third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set.This release automates almost all of the behind-the-scenes work. The boring parts–CRS juggling, extent passing, heightmap repetition, matrix conversion, and other bookkeeping–stay in the package internals. The user is then free to jump to the enjoyable creative roles: the executive producer of the analysis, the production designer of the world, or the sound designer of a multi-sensory data experience.Spatial data: free yourself from the matrix!Rayshader now accepts many more spatial inputs for the heightmap. The function can now accept a heightmap as a matrix, a , a object, or a raster filename. When the input is spatial, rayshader extracts and caches the extent and CRS. If is not supplied, rayshader derives it from raster cell resolution. If the raster is geographic longitude/latitude, rayshader estimates the meter-per-cell scale at the raster center. The data was always there; it just had to be piped around to the right place! Now I do the plumbing for you.Let’s look at an example. The same DEM and main-road data feed both versions below. The difference is who’s now doing the spatial bookkeeping (hint: it’s not you).Internally, rayshader still converts the raster to something it can render. Externally, the scene remembers enough to let the functions just work.There is now also a cleaner division between physical scale and visual exaggeration. now describes the relationship between horizontal and vertical units, while describes the stylistic exaggeration. For spatial rasters, rayshader can derive from the raster itself, placing the data at its physical scale. You can then adjust to emphasize the terrain without changing the underlying unit conversion.And this spatial data directionality can now be reversed. turns a rayshader image, matrix, RGB array, or RGBA array back into a georeferenced . It can inherit the cached extent and CRS from the active scene, convert rayshader’s linear color values to sRGB, and optionally append the source heightmap as an additional raster layer. So rayshader’s output can now feed back into other GIS software, rather than just assume rayshader is the final destination itself.This release lets rayshader fit into a real spatial workflow: spatial input, then rayshader styling, followed by spatial output. So you can generate beautiful hillshades and terrains in R, and then bring them into other spatial software like QGIS or ArcGIS. Work in the GIS interface you already know, render the terrain in R, and drop the result right back into your map.A watershed moment for rayshader waterRayshader’s water was always a bit of an afterthought: it was good for rendering an ocean with bathymetry data, but it didn’t really work if the water was localized to one portion of the map. A lake halfway up a mountain shouldn’t require flooding everything below it to see the water, but rayshader’s old water meshing method assumed one water level for the whole map. Which was perfect if all you needed was that one large body of water: set a level and fill the scene to that height. Separate lakes, reservoirs at different elevations, and imperfect shorelines called for something more flexible.Now water can arrive as a raster or a polygon, high in the mountains or below sea level. uses the terrain and coordinates already stored in the scene to properly place and render the water in a sane way. Water can follow grid cells with water_render_method = "raster" or preserve polygon boundaries with the default, water_render_method = "polygon". Both draw a watertight mesh at the footprint and elevation you supply, even when that means an exposed vertical water wall where the supplied shoreline doesn’t quite meet the terrain. Fast, flexible, and suitable for the rare case where you need to visualize Moses crossing the Red Sea. Figure 6: The optimized method (right) fits its shoreline to the terrain; the raster method (left) uses that exact fitted elevation. Raster edge expansion is disabled () to keep the grid-cell boundary visible–otherwise, the expansion would hide the edges in the ground. Another (much cooler, IMO) option is water_render_method = "optimized". It fits a closed shoreline to the actual 3D terrain mesh, adjusting the water elevation to match the supplied area. Using the elevations beneath your water footprint to seed candidate levels, the optimizer searches for a contour that comes as close as possible to the supplied water area without spilling out of the terrain. The animation below shows how candidate levels change the flooded area. Figure 7: Fitting the lake to its basin: candidate levels change the flooded area. The dark outline follows the actual triangle-clipped water polygon at each candidate level. If no closed water body is possible—for example, the supplied water would flood the entire map—rayshader falls back to raster water.A different problem arises when a DEM has no bathymetry: the lake bed and its surface occupy the same plane. is a new function that can lower the terrain beneath a lake polygon before you add water, making room for the lake instead of letting the surfaces overlap. It can also raise terrain SimCity 2000-style (no tornados or alien invasions… yet).Additionally, in , water can now use a rough dielectric material to spread reflections into the broad highlights you expect from a rippled lake. A perfectly smooth dielectric surface behaves like glass: reflected light stays coherent, so lakes and rivers can turn into polished sheets. Real water has small wind-driven ripples, each reflecting light in a slightly different direction. The microfacet material models this give a more realistic appearance to bodies of water, especially when viewed at a low angle. Figure 8: Glassy water on the left; microfacet water on the right. Rayshader: now streaming!Streams need to follow the terrain as they wind downhill. takes spatial line data, samples the elevation along each path, and builds ribbons of water that hug the surface. Widths can vary by feature, and connected streams can be merged to reduce visible seams in high-quality renders. Put those streams together with lakes and you have a hydrologic scene driven by data.Note that there’s no complex GIS concepts on the rayshader side: all the complexity is related to defining the visual style and appearance. As it should be–rayshader is a visualization package! The remaining complexity is just standard data complexity present in any analysis: get the data loaded, cleaned, and in a form that represents the thing you care about.The road to believable roads3D maps might seem like a fun little toy rather than a serious class of data visualization, but the third dimension is often surprisingly important for understanding geospatial data. This becomes less surprising when you realize that the most common mapping tool used by regular people–GPS apps–use 3D quite extensively. When you’re traveling through a city, buildings give you landmarks to match to your surroundings; on a walking or cycling route, the terrain shows where you’ll be climbing; and at a complex highway interchange, seeing which roads pass over one another helps you follow the right ramp and choose the right exit.I already had surface-hugging polygons working for streams. Swap the water for asphalt and there’s a road! Easy, peasy, right?No! What’s the issue? We’re spoiled with our GPS apps: we’re used to roads looking like roads. A strip of grey asphalt needs lane markings for someone to know it’s a road. With the help of some fun repeating UV coordinate tricks and our new spatial-first workflow, we can paint properly-sized lines on the road at the cost of a few small textures. And we can use the lane counts supplied in OpenStreetMap data to add the correct number of lanes to each road. Rayshader uses those counts to mesh and texture the road, while the scene’s spatial information keeps the markings correctly sized.In Figure 11, each dash is 10 feet long and each gap is 30 feet. Those familiar markings do double duty: they improve the picture and act as little scale bars scattered through the scene. Beautiful! Pack it up, put a bow on it, and move on to the next feature, right?No! Our roads are still smooshed together on one layer. At an interchange, that borders on uninterpretable.OpenStreetMap doesn’t provide a full 3D road model. But it does carry one tiny (but extremely useful!) nugget of vertical information needed to draw roads correctly in 2D: . Draw layer 0, then layer 1, then layer 2, and the right road appears on top. That tells us which road crosses over which; it doesn’t tell us their heights or how the ramps return to ground level. Is this enough information to fully reconstruct our 3D roads?The tempting shortcut is to turn each layer into a fixed height: find the crossings, lift each road by a standard overpass height, and ease it back toward the ground with some sort of ad hoc relaxation rule. What could go wrong?Everything. Everything can go wrong.Simple hacks? Don’t work here. Turns out the world is filled with little annoying complications like a bridge crossing a sunken highway (the highway is already below ground, so the bridge needs no change in elevation), or short segments in interchanges that are technically not stacked but fall between stacked layers, or places where the road is technically stacked over a traversable water body (which also counts as a layer!), or a thousand other pesky little details.What are we to do then? How can we implement realistic highways? It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?The American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) has a design manual for Interstate highways. Two of the things it covers are exactly what our map is missing. How much room does a truck need under a bridge? How steep can the road get on its way up there? Now that rayshader knows the scale of the scene, I can give the solver a clearance in feet and a maximum grade in percent. Here are the default settings I gave the road solver (these are customizable):Keeping crossing road surfaces at least 14 feet apartLimiting the road grade to 7%Ensuring roads default to hugging the ground when not part of an intersection and do not rise unnecessarilyWe can turn these requirements into constraints on the road heights. While the rules aren’t guaranteed to generate roads that match the real-world roads exactly, it’s going to be pretty close: excursions from the bare minimum allowable ruleset will usually only increase cost, and we’re talking government contracts here. Around each interchange, we discretize the roads into short segments and solve for their elevations together: maintain the crossing order and clearance, limit the grades, and keep the roads close to the terrain wherever possible.It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?For example, a road can weave over and under several others. Lifting one crossing changes the grades leading into the next, so solving each crossing independently won’t work–we have to solve all the linked constraints at once. We build a graph of the road connections with {igraph}, locate crossings with {sf}, and follow the constraints along connected road segments. Each connected optimization region gets a sparse quadratic problem, assembled with {Matrix} and solved with {osqp}. It turns out, R has everything you need to build and optimize road profiles.It’s pretty cool how closely a set of road-design rules and OSM’s layer ordering can recreate a complex interchange. The layer tags tell us which road goes over which, and the rules guide how the ramps connect them. Here’s Houston, now modeled in a sane way:Beautiful. And since I went to Houston for this year’s Posit::conf, I was able to drive over specific intersections I rendered here and confirm that yes: the roads were accurately meshed. Minus the traffic.The novelty seeking half of my brain immediately followed this thought with: “You should put in cars now!” to which the logical, killjoy side of my brain responded “NO! STOP IT! YOU’VE IMPLEMENTED TOO MANY FEATURES ALREADY! You will never release this update if you keep indulging yourself! Stop it!”A human battery? No–a human measuring stick.Lane markings made the scale of a scene easier to read. Naturally, that led me to the ultimate human-scale feature: humans! But I couldn’t just throw the first set of free human models I found on the internet into the package. I did a fairly extensive search for a suitable pre-made model with both male and female variants, but to no avail. I had some requirements:Low-poly enough to fit in the package when compressed (an R package is limited to 5 MB).Proportioned like actual people, which rules out a surprising number of free models.I couldn’t find a model that met these requirements with a suitable redistribution license. So I decided this was a great opportunity to learning something new: mesh sculpting in VR! I pulled out my Quest 3 and downloaded Shapelabs, which after a bit of practice and futzing around got me exactly what I wanted. Low-poly, but still human enough that you can read the pose at a glance.From Shapelabs, the models went into Blender as GLB files for rigging and posing, then out as compact OBJ meshes for the package:Male models on a dark blue podium.Female models on a dark red podium. Figure 18: My inspiration for these poses were 1) many hours playing Human Fall Flat, 2) the guy who’s about to crack his head open on every “wet floor” caution sign, and 3) philadelphia Compressed, they’re roughly 18–21 KB each, checking the filesize box. Both model variants stand about 6 feet tall, with consistent proportions across their poses. Finally, a unit of measurement you can relate to!The original was based on a simple idea: take a ggplot2 object, turn a fill or color aesthetic into height, and map the original plot onto that extruded surface. This made it possible to create 3D ggplots without learning a separate 3D plotting API. Just drop in your existing plot and poof! A 3D version would appear.But this came with one limitation: the data had to be attached to the surface.Floating data needs something to ground it. I originally kept the data attached to the surface deliberately: actual 3D data is harder to understand on a 2D screen, since depth is ambiguous. Extruded 2D surfaces provide a continuous underlying substrate, which makes interpretation easier–the surface itself provides depth cues, by nature of surface continuity providing cues on depth ordering. It’s not hard to plop down some floating 3D data in a box and call it a day: before rayshader, that was what pretty much every 3D plotting library I encountered did. In my opinion, that lazy approach helped give 3D dataviz its terrible reputation. Adding 3D data disconnected from that substrate requires additional care and thought to keep the data interpretable.Which rayshader now provides!In rayshader 1.0, is much more tightly integrated with the family of functions that add real 3D data to the scene. Rayshader now extracts the data extent from the existing ggplot2 scene. Basically, we now track how ggplot2 transforms data into the image, so we can use the same transformation for our 3D data. Downstream render calls can use that extent to place real 3D geometry in the correct part of the plot. The ggplot is no longer just a surface extrusion: it’s now the base coordinate system for a complete 3D scene.And this can really help visually, as that surface extrusion wasn’t ideal for certain types of data. The original raster extrusion worked well for smooth surfaces, density plots, and continuous fields, but sharp polygon boundaries and abrupt vertical edges were harder.Take Figure 19: it shows a map of US states with height mapped to population. States share an boundary in the source polygons, but when rasterized to row of pixels, you can see the colors bleed down the step between states. This is an unavoidable problem when you try to force vector data into a raster format. So we avoid it by drawing the actual 3D data. On the right, each state’s own polygon makes a crisp vertical wall.Raster extrusion: transition regions get blurred between colors.Vector extrusion: each state has a continuous polygon edge. Figure 19: State population mapped to the z-axis. The same integration lets individual points float above a flat ggplot2 substrate (enabled with plot_gg(..., flat_substrate = TRUE)). The ggplot establishes the scales and coordinate system, and rayshader adds the observed values as actual 3D points, positioned correctly. gives those floating marks a scale you can read. It picks up the height scale from the ggplot, and you can put the axis inside a panel or along the outer edge of the plot. If you have facets, you can pick the panel. It works on regular terrain maps, too. Figure 20: Each point is one car in . Weight and fuel economy are on 2D ggplot2 axes, and its elevation gives the horsepower (noted in the z-axis). This removes a ton of visual compromises. Instead of forcing every feature to become part of the surface texture, we use the surface texture as the base and add the features as real 3D geometry. The plot layout and elements are still determined by ggplot2: we’re just adding data to the z-axis. Faceted plots can receive geometry one panel at a time. Spatial plots built with carry their geographic transform into the scene, too. Your base plot can use familiar geoms—, , , , or —while rayshader adds polygons, points, paths, and a labeled z-axis in those coordinates.3D ggplots were always a cool, sometimes useful novelty. Now they can be a foundation for complex 3D visualizations. How complex are we talking about? Watch me demo it below with a data visualization showing ADSB flight path data over Washington, DC. Come fly over the National Mall with me and I’ll walk you through how deep the 3D rabbit hole goes.Better buildings, paths, labels, and objectsThe functions have been rewritten around the same principle: spatial data already encodes where it is, so there is no reason to throw that information out. can accept spatial point objects. can accept spatial line objects. can accept points, multipoints, polygons, and multipolygons, converting polygon inputs to centroids when needed. and render_beveled_polygons() use cached heightmap and extent metadata. uses spatial footprints, roof materials, roof angles, height columns, and CRS-aware extent filtering. can place OBJ models using spatial point data. You can see most of these in action in Figure 22.There’s some new basic hillshading options as well. adds an RGBA haze overlay based on an exponential atmospheric model. It is useful for low-elevation haze, valley haze, and scenes where you want the atmosphere to participate in the map rather than sit behind it. It is a good way to subtly separate mountain tops from valleys. Figure 23: Haze fades in and out as the terrain rotates, softening low valleys while leaving higher ground clearer. renders a top-down radiance pass from a cached hillshade context, the active 3D scene, or a supplied heightmap. It gives 2D maps and 3D ggplot2 workflows access to more visually-striking physically based lighting without forcing the entire project into a final path-traced render. This is a nice way to get higher-quality shadows on a model you can still rotate and revise quickly. The result is still an RGBA overlay, so it can be composited back into the usual rayshader map pipeline or exported to other programs.For a small area, we can usually ignore Earth’s curvature. As a map grows to cover hundreds or thousands of kilometers, the bend of the Earth can become an important part of the story. For satellite orbits, long-distance flight paths, and regional coverage maps, curvature can help signal to the reader that we’re dealing with global-scale data without an explicit scale bar.Setting in adds that curvature to the scene. Mountains and valleys can look flatter beside the much larger bend of the Earth when no vertical exaggeration is applied, but the adjustment gives those other GIS layers a more useful spatial context. Figure 25: Alaska and its neighbors with a flat surface (left) and Earth curvature enabled (right). For example, Figure 25 shows three Starlink satellites cross Alaska along paths calculated from real orbital data. Their simulated beams track populated places below, switching targets as they move within reach. Both views show the same moment, but on the right, the surface and orbital altitudes are adjusted to match the global curvature. This helps give the viewer important context clues for the spatial scales we’re dealing with here that the flat projection does not provide.Even higher quality Want to realistically light a scene at a very specific time and date? Just give rayshader a date and time–it already knows the place. For a scene with cached spatial coordinates, render_highquality(datetime = ...) can infer the location and generate the corresponding sky and sunlight. You don’t need to look up the latitude, longitude, or sun angle again. Depending on the sky model, that can include stars, planets, and the moon’s phase and brightness.As an example, around the equinoxes, the low sun lines up with the National Mall’s east–west axis—a favorite alignment for photographers. On March 25, 2026, at 6:56:11 p.m. EDT, the modeled shadow of the Washington Monument runs parallel to the Mall’s main paths. A few days past the equinox, the sun is still high enough at that alignment to keep the shadow within this view.And separately, text and annotation lines were physical objects in the rendered scene. Their letters and lines cast shadows across the terrain and buildings, giving annotations the same simulated weight as the things they were annotating. A label should help you read the map without becoming another object in it. Figure 27: Mount Rainier, Mount St. Helens, and Mount Adams turn with the terrain, but their labels always face you. The leader lines stay anchored to the volcano locations. Terrain heights use 4× vertical exaggeration. The labels in Figure 27 are drawn in screen space: their positions stay attached to the map, while the text keeps its size and faces the camera throughout the orbit, without casting shadows over the volcanoes. The horsepower axis in Figure 20 uses the same approach. The lines and text are composited in real time when you’re looking at the high quality preview render in rayrender, so you can set up the shot exactly how you want to. Oh, and you can set now as well, which removes the sample timer so you can have all the time in the world to set up your render. This is especially important now, since rayrender is now fully GPU-accellerated on ARM macs, leading to 30-50x speedups in rendering performance, so your render can often end before you got a chance to click on the screen. This blog post, however, is about rayshader, so I won’t steal its thunder talking about the awesome improvements in rayrender :)It’s been a long, properly textured road–why 1.0 after eight years? I now feel that rayshader has firmly found its niche and purpose, and this overhaul feels like a graduation moment for the package. I’m no longer figuring out what a 3D GIS workflow in R should feel like–it’s now about making that workflow work for you. And thinking about all the people who used rayshader to produce everything from beautiful generative art and frameable cartographic works to scientific articles and award winning journalism made me decide to give rayshader the graduation it deserves, and make sure it knows: You’re number 1.0!The grand finale and most exciting part of any publication: the bibliography.Rayshader wouldn’t be possible without the work of all the packages and people that supported it and provided great user feedback during its development. In a normal blog post, this is where normally you’d have a list of citations and people to thank. But how often does R’s most cinematic package get a 1.0 release? I decided the people, packages, and data behind rayshader deserved the full cinematic treatment that rayshader has provided the R ecosystem. And that the cinematic treatment should be created entirely in R, using rayrender, of course. Please stick around and hit play for the credits below—and be sure to turn the sound on.
